doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

title: Pick-up bands sell the music short; Bob's organization
summary: She says pick-up groups shortchange the music, and contrasts Bob's organized approach at Mat Domber's jazz party.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: you’re Jelly Roll Morton or if you’re King Oliver or Louis Armstrong or Sidney Bechet. But not everybody is, sad to say.
Do you think it sells the music short?

Yes I do. Yes I do. I think that people think if that’s all there is, maybe that is one of the problems that we have today. I mean at least the way that it sounded with the rose hip thorn, the rose thorn, it wasn’t great, but at least we were listening to the right stuff. If you’re hearing something that’s been so adulterated down, down, down, down, down, sort of it’s not going to sound as good. And how can you sound — as Bob always says, I quote Bob a lot, but he says you’re only as good as the people you play with. And if you’re picking up somebody that’s just done a ten hour shift down the mine, as diligent and as enthusiastic as he may well be, he’s not going to have the same kind of energy to put on a concert and be in sync with you, do you think?
I doubt it. I think of that kind of situation, even at the jazz parties that exist in this country, where all the musicians certainly are of high caliber, but I would prefer at times to hear some—

Organized bands. Well just this past March, Mat Domber did March of Jazz. We had a number of sets. We had some wonderful sets. We had sets with Dave McKenna and Dick Hyman, Antti Sarpila, we had wonderful people. But there’s one thing that I just — I cannot speak highly enough of Bob, but he is an organized person. He’s organized in his personal life, and he’s organized in his musical life, it’s one and the same. And before you go on stage there is never a matter of sort of what should we play next. “Undecided” no I don’t want to play that — well I don’t do it in that key, it’s never like that. We all know what we’re going to do. There’s always a time when Bob probably fumbles trying to get the program out of his pocket and —
